text_blocks.snippet: Early signs of type 2 diabetes often develop slowly over years, meaning many people do not notice them at first.

list.snippet: Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar forces your kidneys to work overtime to clear excess glucose, making you pee more often (especially at night) and feel very thirsty.
Constant fatigue: Your cells cannot absorb glucose properly for energy, leaving you feeling exhausted even after sleeping.
Increased hunger: You may feel hungry shortly after eating because your body is not getting the fuel it needs from food.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar can change the shape of the lenses in your eyes, causing temporary blurry sight.
Slow-healing cuts and sores: Elevated sugar levels impair blood flow and nerve function, making minor wounds take much longer to heal.
Frequent infections: Bacteria and yeast thrive on excess glucose, leading to recurring urinary tract or yeast infections.
Tingling or numbness: Nerve irritation or damage can cause a prickling sensation or numbness in your hands and feet.
Darkened skin patches: Velvety, dark skin folds—known as acanthosis nigricans on the neck or armpits—can signal insulin resistance.

text_blocks.snippet: You can learn more about recognizing these red flags through the Mayo Clinic or review guidance provided by Diabetes.org.
